title: Reaching it: links, ports and who can open them
standfirst: A machine nobody can reach is not an agent. There are four doors in — an HTTPS link, a raw TCP port, SSH, and the provider's API — and the important difference is who can open each one.
idea: Every provider gives you an HTTPS address for a port inside the machine. What differs is the lock. A provider-key link needs an API key or a signed token on every request. A token-in-the-URL link is a password you can paste: convenient, and exactly as safe as the place you pasted it. An open link has no lock at all.

The open case is more common than buyers expect. boxd's name.boxd.sh is public to the internet with no authentication in front of it. InstaBox's public ports are unauthenticated by design, though a port can instead be made private behind a token. Agent 37's public port is deliberately credential-free and keeps working until you delete it. In each case the URL is the only secret.

The other doors are less visible. SSH is sometimes a real port, sometimes a WebSocket tunnel, sometimes a shell over the provider's own transport. Raw TCP exists at a few providers and is missing at most. The provider's API is always a door, and sometimes the only one.

splits.heading: Token in the URL, or no token at all
body: Sandboxer puts a token in the preview URL by default and strips it before the request reaches your app. Lizard uses one token per sandbox, so a link to one port opens every exposed port on that machine. Sprites makes the URL private to the organisation, reachable with an org token.
At boxd and InstaBox the URL is the only credential. Agent 37 goes further and sells an explicitly public port that anyone can reach with no credential at all.

splits.heading: Raw TCP and SSH are a separate capability
body: Runtime, boxd and Boat support a raw TCP path; Boat's depends on IPv4, which is not guaranteed. Sandboxer and InstaBox route SSH through a gateway. Lizard has no SSH protocol at all: its ssh command is an interactive shell over the provider's transport, so scp, rsync and port forwarding do not work.
Vercel exposes web ports and bills traffic to them, but a general raw TCP inbound or a personal SSH endpoint is not published.

splits.heading: A sleeping machine changes the answer
body: A URL that wakes a machine is a different product from a URL that returns an error. Sprites, Runtime and InstaBox document wake on request. boxd's bot protection gates the wake: a webhook, API client or uptime monitor gets a 503 check page and the machine does not wake.
Boat cannot wake on a URL at all, because a stop removed the machine.

watchFor: Who can open the link: only you, anyone you send it to, or anyone who guesses it.
Whether the token is per port or per machine.
Whether a request to a sleeping machine wakes it or returns an error.
Whether raw TCP and SSH exist, and whether SSH is a real port or a tunnel.
Whether the URL survives a stop and resume.

rows.scenario: Instance and preview URLs need an API key or a signed URL; the public port is deliberately open to anyone and keeps working.
rows.note: Every port gets an HTTPS URL; instance and preview URLs require an API key or a time-boxed signed URL. A public port is deliberately unauthenticated and permanent. SSH is tunnelled; no raw TCP.

source.quote: **Instance URLs require auth on every request**

rows.scenario: Preview URLs back a running sandbox with optional auth; whether auth is on by default is not published.
rows.note: Specific ports can be exposed, and preview URLs back a running sandbox with optional auth and custom domains. Default ingress authentication is not published.

source.quote: Render an application in real-time through a direct preview URL backed by a running Blaxel sandbox, with optional auth and custom domains.

rows.scenario: The HTTPS route is token-gated unless you pass --public, and SSH is a real port.
rows.note: An HTTPS route per port, token-gated by default and --public to remove it; SSH on port 22; raw TCP by opening the sandbox firewall, but only IPv6 is guaranteed.

source.quote: boat does not support custom domains.

rows.scenario: Every machine answers on name.boxd.sh with no authentication; bot protection only gates the wake, so a sleeping machine returns a check page.
rows.note: Every machine is on name.boxd.sh with no authentication in front of it; subdomain proxies add ports, up to three raw TCP forwards, and SSH on a dedicated port. Bot protection only gates wake-ups.

source.quote: When a request would wake a sleeping machine, boxd first asks the visitor to pass a quick browser check.

rows.scenario: There is no URL to paste: the client reaches the page through your Worker, and any authentication is code you write.
rows.note: HTTP from the internet reaches the instance only through your Worker. No built-in preview auth, token or IP allowlist. SSH exists only through Wrangler, does not start a stopped container and does not keep one alive.

source.quote: The server has no public port, so your Worker forwards requests to it.

rows.scenario: The preview URL needs authentication unless the sandbox is public; the standard token opens the whole sandbox and cannot be revoked.
rows.note: Preview links are authenticated unless `public` is true. The standard token is sandbox-wide, opens the terminal and toolbox, and cannot be revoked; signed URLs are per port, 60 seconds by default and 24 hours maximum.

source.quote: If a sandbox has its `public` property set to `true`, preview links are publicly accessible without authentication. Otherwise, authentication is required.

rows.scenario: Anyone who has the URL gets in; there is no authentication by default.
rows.note: Public URLs are reachable by anyone who knows them, with no authentication by default. SSH runs through a WebSocket proxy rather than a native port.

source.quote: By default, a sandbox's public URLs are reachable by anyone who knows them.

rows.scenario: A port can be public, or private so it answers only requests that carry its token, which can be replaced.
rows.note: An HTTPS link per port, up to 16, either public or private behind a replaceable token. SSH and mosh go through a gateway. Raw non-web ports are in an admin-only preview, later paid plans only with 5 per workspace. No custom domain.

source.quote: A **private** port answers only requests that carry its token.

rows.scenario: One token per sandbox opens every exposed port on it, so a link to the demo also opens the rest.
rows.note: A preview URL per exposed port, gated by one token per sandbox that opens every port on it. WebSockets pass through. No raw TCP, no SSH protocol, no custom domains for sandboxes.

source.quote: The token belongs to the sandbox, not to a port: it opens every port you expose on that sandbox

rows.scenario: Nothing is reachable until a port is exposed; the client needs a connect token, and the container sees a verified header.
rows.note: No inbound by default. Expose encrypted, h2 or unencrypted ports; connect tokens are the recommended path for HTTP and WebSockets, and raw TCP is possible. `inbound_cidr_allowlist` is not enforced on unencrypted tunnels.

source.quote: You can make authenticated HTTP and WebSocket requests to a Sandbox by generating Sandbox Connect Tokens.

rows.scenario: An HTTP service can be exposed through the API, but default authentication is not published.
rows.note: An instance can expose an HTTP service through the API. Default authentication and raw TCP support are not published.

rows.scenario: Nothing is reachable until you open a door; a token-gated preview is one of the options.
rows.note: Nothing is reachable until you open a door: token-gated previews, custom domains, raw TCP ports, a WireGuard or Tailscale private network, or SSH over the API.

source.quote: Nothing on the internet can connect in to a sandbox. These are the ways in. You open each one yourself

rows.scenario: A token sits in the preview URL by default and is stripped before the request reaches the app.
rows.note: A stable HTTPS address per port, private by default with a token in the URL; --public removes it. A public IPv6 with the firewall closed except SSH. No raw-TCP endpoint.

source.quote: Private (default) | `https://…-3000.box.sandboxer.com?_token=…` | Anyone with the full URL.

rows.scenario: The URL is private to the organisation and needs an org token, so a client outside it cannot open the link.
rows.note: Every Sprite has an HTTPS URL that is private to the organisation by default, reachable with an org token. SSH requires installing a server and proxying it.

source.quote: A Sprite URL is private by default. It's reachable only by members of your org, through the browser or with an org token

rows.scenario: Web ports can be exposed, up to 15, and traffic to them is billable; no general inbound TCP is published.
rows.note: Web ports can be exposed, up to 15 per sandbox, and traffic to them is billable. The dashboard's Connect tab gives a terminal in the browser. A general raw TCP inbound, standard SSH or public IPv4 is not published.

source.quote: Data your sandbox sends to the internet, plus all traffic to and from exposed ports, is billable and measured in GB.

rows.figure: HTTPS per port; auth on by default
rows.scenario: Each exposed port gets `https://<port>-<name>.sandbox.tensorlake.ai`; a project key is required unless the sandbox is switched to public access.
rows.note: The proxy carries HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC, and preserves path and query. Auth is the default: requests need a project API key, or a signed-in session cookie from a browser. `allow_unauthenticated_access` makes exposed user ports public, but the management API on port 9501 always requires auth.

source.quote: `https://<port>-<sandbox-id-or-name>.sandbox.tensorlake.ai` routes to a user service listening on `<port>` inside the sandbox

rows.scenario: The agent's port 3000 is reachable at the Droplet's public IP with nothing in front of it; SSH and a browser console are both there.
rows.note: A public IPv4 per Droplet, real SSH, a browser console and any TCP port except SMTP. There is no tokenised preview link and no port-forwarding service; standard ssh -L works. The OpenClaw image adds a gateway token and TLS in front of its own port.

source.quote: By default, each Droplet you create comes with its own public IPv4 address.

scenario.title: Paste the preview URL into a client channel
scenario.setup: The agent builds a demo on port 3000. You copy the HTTPS address and paste it into a shared channel for a client, who opens it the next morning from a different country.

beats.what: You copy the URL. Whether it carries a token, and whether that token covers one port or the whole machine, is already decided.
The machine goes idle or stops. The link either wakes it, returns an error, or points at a machine that no longer exists.
The client opens the link. Anyone with the URL, or only someone holding a key, gets through.

scenario.turn: Four providers here put no authentication in front of the port at all, and one makes the token per machine rather than per port. A URL that wakes a sleeping machine is a different product from one that returns an error.

questions: Is there authentication in front of a preview URL by default, or is the URL the only secret?
Is the token per port or per machine, and can it be revoked without recreating the sandbox?
Does a request to a sleeping machine wake it, or return an error page?
Does the URL survive a stop and resume, and does it change when the machine is recreated?
Is SSH a real port or a tunnel, and is raw TCP inbound available at all?
